exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle
model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle
model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]:

(i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a
constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied
rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with
four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph
of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of
motion

$$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$

where $\Phi$ is the raised-index operator of the field at the event $x(\tau)$,
defined by $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently
$m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. Here $dU/d\tau$ is the derivative of $U$
with respect to proper time, that is, the four-acceleration of the worldline
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The particle's own field
is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no
self-force.

(ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of
[[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated
matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density
$\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit
W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the
spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local
interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed
current alone.

(iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within
electromagnetism. The coupling is adopted for constant $q$ and $m>0$; no
magnetic-monopole coupling, no radiation reaction and no self-force are
included. In particular the nonrelativistic coordinate statement
$mr''=q(E+r'\times B)$ is not adopted as exact: the adopted statement is the
covariant one of clause (i), and any low-speed statement requires its own
approximation hypotheses and error bounds.

exact_citation_checks.quote:
**Regularity convention for a possibly non-open parameter interval.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $k\in\mathbb N$. A map on $U\times I$ is **jointly $C^k$** when it is the restriction of a $C^k$ map on some open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; it is **jointly $C^\infty$** when it is the restriction of one smooth map on such an open neighbourhood. For open $I$ these are exactly the usual open-domain classes; at included endpoints of a nondegenerate interval, time derivatives are the corresponding relative one-sided derivatives. For empty or singleton $I$ the convention still asserts extension existence and the spatial identities below, but it does not determine time jets uniquely from the restricted values alone. The convention does not require a fixed uniform enlargement of an unbounded $I$.

**Vector witness.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a\in U$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Then

$$A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr)\times(x-a)\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the curl being taken in the spatial variables and the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

**Scalar witness.** If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$, then

$$\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\bigl\langle C\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr),\,x-a\bigr\rangle\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the gradient and inner product being those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For jointly $C^\infty$ data both potentials are jointly $C^\infty$. No global potential on a non-star-shaped open set is claimed, and the fields $B(\cdot,t)$ and $C(\cdot,t)$ need not be continuous in $t$ at endpoints beyond the stated one-sided convention.

located_uses.restatement: [L4] For $|\beta|<1$ the passive boost acts in the $(0,1)$-plane by $x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$, $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$; it is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\beta)$, so the ordered basis $e'_a:=B(\beta)^{-1}e_a$ is $\eta$-orthonormal, future and positively oriented and is the basis of an inertial frame whose chart satisfies $x'=B(\beta)\circ x$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], [[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

formulation_use:
**(c)** For a passive boost with parameter $b$ along the $x^1$ direction the
block of $B(b)$ in the $(0,1)$-plane is $\gamma\begin{pmatrix}1&-b\\-b&1\end{pmatrix}$
with $\gamma=(1-b^2)^{-1/2}$
([[def-lorentz-boost]]), whose determinant is $\gamma^2(1-b^2)=1$. Let $x'$ be
the chart of the inertial frame related to $x$ by this boost, so that
$x'=B(b)\circ x$
([[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]],
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]],
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]); the coordinate image of the diamond in
$x'$ is the parallelogram with centre $\gamma(1,-b)$ and half-diagonal vectors
$\gamma(1,-b)$ and $\gamma(-b,1)$, whose area is
$2\gamma^2(1-b^2)=2$ m$^2$. Hence the area of the diamond in the
$(x^0,x^1)$-plane is the same in the chart of every frame related to $x$ by such
a boost; this is the source's invariance of the area of a light-rectangle.

exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

which on a compact interval containing $a$ and $s_0$ is the value at $b$ of the
integral function with base point $a$ of the integrand
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**Scope.** The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: at a
null point the integrand vanishes, so the integral is constant; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.

exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L:\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L:L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

formulation_use:
**(c)** For a passive boost with parameter $b$ along the $x^1$ direction the
block of $B(b)$ in the $(0,1)$-plane is $\gamma\begin{pmatrix}1&-b\\-b&1\end{pmatrix}$
with $\gamma=(1-b^2)^{-1/2}$
([[def-lorentz-boost]]), whose determinant is $\gamma^2(1-b^2)=1$. Let $x'$ be
the chart of the inertial frame related to $x$ by this boost, so that
$x'=B(b)\circ x$
([[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]],
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]],
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]); the coordinate image of the diamond in
$x'$ is the parallelogram with centre $\gamma(1,-b)$ and half-diagonal vectors
$\gamma(1,-b)$ and $\gamma(-b,1)$, whose area is
$2\gamma^2(1-b^2)=2$ m$^2$. Hence the area of the diamond in the
$(x^0,x^1)$-plane is the same in the chart of every frame related to $x$ by such
a boost; this is the source's invariance of the area of a light-rectangle.

exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\},$$

which is the $C^\infty$ case of the bounded $C^k$ graph domain of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open set with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$. Then there exists a real-linear operator $E_\Omega$, determined only by $\Omega$, a finite smooth atlas and fixed cutoffs, such that for every open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and every function $u:\Omega\times J\to\mathbb R$ that is of class $C^\infty$ on the open set $\Omega\times J$ and whose every mixed derivative $D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j u:\Omega\times J\to\mathbb R$ has a continuous extension to $\overline\Omega\times J$ ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), the function $E_\Omega u$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times J$, satisfies $E_\Omega u(x,\tau)=u(x,\tau)$ for all $(x,\tau)\in\overline\Omega\times J$ and

$$D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j(E_\Omega u)\big|_{\overline\Omega\times J}=\text{the continuous extension of }D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j u$$

for all multi-indices $\alpha$ and all $j\ge0$, and is spatially supported in one fixed compact subset of $V$, in the sense that there is a compact $K_\Omega\subseteq V$ with $E_\Omega u(x,\tau)=0$ for all $x\notin K_\Omega$, $\tau\in J$. For every compact $K\subseteq J$, every integer $m\ge0$ and every $j\ge0$,

$$\sup_{\tau\in K}\|\partial_\tau^j E_\Omega u(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^m(\mathbb R^3)}\le C_m\sup_{\tau\in K}\|\partial_\tau^j u(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^m(\overline\Omega)},$$

where $\|w\|_{C^m(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|D^\alpha w(x)|$ and $\|W\|_{C^m(\mathbb R^3)}:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^3}|D^\alpha W(x)|$, and the constant $C_m$ depends only on $m$, $\Omega$, the atlas and cutoffs. The extension commutes with every time derivative: $\partial_\tau^j(E_\Omega u)=E_\Omega(\partial_\tau^j u)$ for all $j\ge0$. No bound uniform over an unbounded $J$ is asserted. Vector-valued inputs of finite dimension are extended componentwise. The construction adds no choice principle: the finite atlas is selected from the cover of all admissible smooth chart patches, finite cutoffs come from the published choice-free compact cutoff lemma, and the infinite coefficient sequence is defined by the explicit formula below. exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes $\delta$ and $\times$. The only
$\eta$-invariant structure of the model remains $\eta$; the Euclidean spatial
structure is not an additional invariant of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$.

formulation_use:
Let $c>0$ and let $x:[a,b]\to A$ be a future timelike worldline with $a<b$
([[def-interval]]) that is piecewise $C^1$ with partition
$a=s_0<s_1<\dots<s_m=b$ in the weak sense of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], with future timelike interior
tangents and finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents. Put $p:=x(a)$,
$q:=x(b)$ and $d:=q-p$. Then $d$ is future timelike. More precisely, writing
$\xi^a:=x_A^a\circ x$ for the coordinate path of the chart $x_A$ of any inertial
frame, one has
$$\xi^0(b)-\xi^0(a)>0\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\xi_{\mathrm{vec}}(b)-\xi_{\mathrm{vec}}(a)|<\xi^0(b)-\xi^0(a),$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean spatial norm of
[[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]. Consequently $p\ne q$,
the number $\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)}$ is a positive real number, and in every inertial
chart the time component of $d$ is positive and dominates the Euclidean norm of
its spatial part, which is exactly the coordinate description of future
timelikeness in that chart. No completeness, compactness beyond the given compact
interval, or choice principle is used.

[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], with a finite partition
$a = s_0 < \cdots < s_m = b$, $C^{1}$ on each open piece and finite one-sided
difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of each piece. Assume its tangents
are nonzero future causal at every open-piece point and at each one-sided
endpoint.

In any inertial chart ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) write
$y = (y^{0},z)$, $z \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$, for the coordinate path. On a piece
$(\alpha,\beta)$, choose $r \in (\alpha,\beta)$; for a function $g$ continuous
there, write

$$\int_{(\alpha,\beta)} g \;:=\; \lim_{u \downarrow \alpha} \int_u^{r} g \;+\; \lim_{v \uparrow \beta} \int_r^{v} g$$

when both limits are finite. Then:

**(a)** $y$ is continuous on $[\alpha,\beta]$, $y^{0'} \ge |z'| \ge 0$ on
$(\alpha,\beta)$, and $y^{0'} > 0$ there.

**(b)** Every coordinate derivative is absolutely improperly Riemann integrable
(its absolute value has finite improper integral), and its signed improper
integral equals the corresponding endpoint increment. The continuous functions
$|z'|$ and $f = \sqrt{(y^{0'})^{2} - |z'|^{2}} = \sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$ have
finite nonnegative improper integrals, with
$\int_{(\alpha,\beta)} f \le \int_{(\alpha,\beta)} y^{0'} = y^{0}(\beta) - y^{0}(\alpha)$.

**(c)** The improper values are independent of $r$, additive under subdivision,
and the finite piece sums are independent of the admissible partition.

**(d)** $D = x(b)-x(a)$ is nonzero future causal: $D^{0} > 0$ and
$|D_{\mathrm{spatial}}| \le D^{0}$ in every inertial chart. If some interior or
one-sided endpoint tangent is future timelike, then $D$ is future timelike.
Coordinate time is strictly increasing on every nondegenerate subinterval. The
integrals need not be ordinary closed-piece Riemann integrals. No
derivative-limit hypothesis, Lebesgue-integration premise, clock identification,
or choice principle is used.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

The prescribed quasistatic external charge-transfer work is $dW_{\rm ext}=\sum_jV_j(s)\,dQ_j(s)=\sum_j(sV_j)Q_j(V)\,ds=s\,ds\sum_jV_jQ_j(V)$, and summing over the conductors and integrating over $s\in[0,1]$ gives $W_{\rm ext}=\bigl(\int_0^1s\,ds\bigr)\sum_jV_jQ_j(V)=\frac12\sum_jV_jQ_j(V)=U$ by [F6] and [step 3.1]. The family is an accounting prescription on the fixed geometry with grounded reference: the potentials vary during assembly, only the final potentials and geometry are fixed, and the sheet-charge accounting is derived directly rather than from the volume-source theorem [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]]; the path-work identity of [F6] gives the endpoint potential-drop reading along any interior piecewise $C^1$ path, with boundary endpoints understood as limits of the continuous closure traces. formulation_use:
Assume the Axiom of Choice for the cited unit-Dirichlet solvability and trace interfaces, and its Countable Choice consequence for surface and integral interfaces ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(\Omega;D_1,\dots,D_m;\Omega_v)$ be the conductor geometry of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], additionally with $\Omega$ a bounded $C^\infty$ ambient domain and $\Omega_v$ connected and with the **outer boundary $\partial\Omega$ grounded**: the data on $\partial\Omega$ are the constant Dirichlet datum $0$; let $\rho_v\equiv0$ on $\Omega_v$ (the pure capacitor configuration: no volume source), and let the framework constants be those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ let $\varphi_j\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ be the unit-potential solution of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-existence]](c) with the smooth data
$$\varphi_j|_{\partial D_k}=\delta_{jk},\qquad \varphi_j|_{\partial\Omega}=0,$$
so that $-\Delta\varphi_j=0$ on $\Omega_v$ with the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], and let $\nu$ be the outward normal of $\Omega_v$ (so on $\partial D_j$ the normal $\nu$ points into the conductor). Define the **capacitance matrix** by
$$C_{jk}:=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\frac{\partial\varphi_k}{\partial\nu}\,dS,\qquad j,k=1,\dots,m,$$
the flux integrals of continuous functions over the compact embedded hypersurfaces $\partial D_j$ (normal derivative of [[def-classical-normal-derivative]]) ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]]). Then:
(a) [Linearity and matrix form] for every $V=(V_1,\dots,V_m)\in\mathbb R^m$ the unique equilibrium potential with conductor potentials $V$ and grounded outer boundary is $\varphi^V=\sum_{j=1}^mV_j\varphi_j$, and the conductor charges of [[pthm-em-conductor-surface-charge]](d) are
$$Q_j(V)=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\frac{\partial\varphi^V}{\partial\nu}\,dS=\sum_{k=1}^mC_{jk}V_k,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad Q=CV.$$
(b) [Reciprocity] $C$ is symmetric: $C_{jk}=C_{kj}$ for all $j,k$; the symmetry is Green's symmetric pairing of the harmonic potentials $\varphi_j,\varphi_k$.
(c) [Energy identity] the field energy of the configuration is
$$U(V)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\Omega_v}|\nabla\varphi^V|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac12V^{T}CV=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^mV_jQ_j(V),$$
and $U(V)>0$ for every $V\ne0$: $C$ is symmetric positive definite. In particular $U(V)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $V=0$, so every nonzero conductor-potential data set stores positive field energy.
(d) [Two-conductor reading] with only conductor $1$ driven and every other conductor grounded, $V=te_1$: $Q_1=C_{11}t$, $Q_j=C_{j1}t$ for $j\ne1$, and $U=\tfrac12C_{11}t^2=\tfrac12Q_1V_1=Q_1^2/(2C_{11})$; the **capacitance of the arrangement** at conductor $1$ with respect to the grounded reference is the positive geometric number $C_{11}>0$, with $C_{11}=Q_1/V_1$ when $t=V_1\ne0$, and the energy identities $U=\tfrac12QV=Q^2/(2C)=\tfrac12CV^2$ hold with $C=C_{11}$, $Q=Q_1$, $V=V_1$. $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the surface-measure interface inherited from [[def-em-surface-distribution]]
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\mathcal D'(U)$ be the space of
distributions on $U$ ([[def-distribution]],
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]); recall that the pairing
$\langle T,\psi\rangle$ is bilinear with no conjugation and that the
distributional partial derivatives are
$\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$
([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(a) [Fields as distributions] Locally integrable fields and source densities on
$U$ are identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

(b) [Point sources] Let $I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval,
let $z:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory whose graph map
$\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ is proper into the open set $U$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$
(coulombs). By [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],

$$\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$ with
$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=0$. If instead
$I_0=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the
absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite and both endpoint
events lie in $U$, the same formulas define distributions with

$$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$$

([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); a finite-history point source
therefore contributes an endpoint term unless that term is included
explicitly, and the pairings above exclude it only by the stated properness or
endpoint hypotheses.

(c) [Stationary-sheet sources] Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded
$C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side
$\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]],
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), and let
$\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous
with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a tangential surface current
density; the sheet is stationary). Then

$$\langle\rho_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_S\sigma(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_SK(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$: for $\psi$ with compact support the inner
integrals are continuous in $t$ on a compact parameter interval and the
functionals are bounded by
$(\sup|\sigma\psi|)\,\mathrm{area}(S)\,\mathrm{length}$ of the time projection
of the support, and likewise in the vector case. A normal sheet current (one
with $K\cdot n\ne0$), a line current and a moving sheet are not source types of
this definition.

(d) [Unrestricted weak fields and optional interface branches] The general
field class for the solution predicate (e) consists of all locally integrable
pairs $(E,B)$ on $U$, also when the source has a stationary-sheet part. No
classical one-sided trace or off-sheet $C^1$ regularity is required to define
those four distributional pairings. Additional trace hypotheses are optional
hypotheses of interface and jump results, not admission requirements of the
general weak model.

one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time, with the explicit additional
conditions that the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the field traces are measurable and locally
integrable on $S\times I$ for $dS\,dt$. This branch supports sheet-distribution

pointwise spatial identities for almost every time, and joint continuity of

four identities are the same as the locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. That earlier postulate explicitly excludes point
and sheet distributions and does not imply their physical adoption here;
adoption for the declared singular-source models is made separately, after
this definition. No physical field equation is deduced merely from defining
this predicate.

chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side
$\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), and let
$\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous
with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a tangential surface current
density). Let $E,B$ be locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$ and $C^1$ on
$(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$ with the following explicit joint one-sided
regularity: around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side is the restriction
of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the corresponding
closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. Thus the fields and their
first space and time derivatives extend continuously to that side of
$S\times I$, locally uniformly on compact cylinders, and let $\rho_v,J_v$ be
continuous on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$ and locally integrable on
$\Omega\times I$. Write $[F]=F_+-F_-$ for the jump of the one-sided traces of
such a field $F$.

Under the separate singular-source physical adoption
[[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], suppose that $E,B$ satisfy the weak
Maxwell equations with the source pair

$$\rho=\rho_v+\rho_S,\qquad J=J_v+J_S,$$

where $(\rho_S,J_S)$ is the stationary-sheet source of
[[def-em-weak-sources]](c) with densities $\sigma,K$ and the pairings there, in
the sense of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e), and where the volume parts
$\rho_v,J_v$ are identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Then, pointwise
on $S\times I$,

$$n\cdot[E]=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad n\times[B]=\mu_0K,\qquad n\cdot[B]=0,\qquad n\times[E]=0,$$

with the ordinary Euclidean inner and cross products of the one-sided traces
([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Equivalently, the surface current density is
$K=(\mu_0)^{-1}\,n\times[B]$ and the surface charge density is
$\sigma=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot[E]$.

The theorem assumes a stationary interface: the hypersurface $S$ and its
normal do not depend on $t$, so the one-sided $C^1$ traces also make
$\partial_tE$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally
integrable, contributing no delta terms. No magnetic surface charge or
magnetic surface current is present in the sources, and correspondingly the
last two identities assert the absence of magnetic sheet delta terms. A moving
interface, a normal sheet current, or a sheet whose support changes with time
is outside this statement and would require additional terms.

full locally integrable field and source class, without asserting undefined
classical trace values. If instead of the joint extension condition the fields

$$\int_I\int_S\bigl(n\cdot[E]-\sigma/\varepsilon_0\bigr)\psi\,dS\,dt,\quad\int_I\int_S(n\cdot[B])\psi\,dS\,dt,\quad\int_I\int_S(n\times[E])\cdot\psi\,dS\,dt,\quad\int_I\int_S\bigl(n\times[B]-\mu_0K\bigr)\cdot\psi\,dS\,dt$$

surface-and-time integrals, with no product of distributions formed; these

since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, they hold for

**Regularity convention for a possibly non-open parameter interval.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $k\in\mathbb N$. A map on $U\times I$ is **jointly $C^k$** when it is the restriction of a $C^k$ map on some open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; it is **jointly $C^\infty$** when it is the restriction of one smooth map on such an open neighbourhood. For open $I$ these are exactly the usual open-domain classes; at included endpoints of a nondegenerate interval, time derivatives are the corresponding relative one-sided derivatives. For empty or singleton $I$ the convention still asserts extension existence and the spatial identities below, but it does not determine time jets uniquely from the restricted values alone. The convention does not require a fixed uniform enlargement of an unbounded $I$.

**Vector witness.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a\in U$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Then

$$A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr)\times(x-a)\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the curl being taken in the spatial variables and the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

**Scalar witness.** If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$, then

$$\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\bigl\langle C\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr),\,x-a\bigr\rangle\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the gradient and inner product being those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For jointly $C^\infty$ data both potentials are jointly $C^\infty$. No global potential on a non-star-shaped open set is claimed, and the fields $B(\cdot,t)$ and $C(\cdot,t)$ need not be continuous in $t$ at endpoints beyond the stated one-sided convention.

(a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement
$$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

(b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$
pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$.

and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and

$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

orientation of the spatial basis; the changes of inertial description adopted
for this framework are proper and orientation preserving, so
orientation-reversing descriptions are not among them.

a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

exact_citation_checks.quote:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] A **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

formulation_use: (e) [Physics reading: ideal grounded plane in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]] the ideal grounded conducting half-space $\{x_3<0\}$ with the field $E_I$ on $H$, $E\equiv0$ below $\Pi$ and the induced density $\sigma:=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+|_\Pi=-\varepsilon_0\,\partial_3\varphi_I|_\Pi$ (using the normal $n=e_3$ from the conductor into the vacuum; $\sigma\in C^\infty(\Pi)$) is a model of the same equilibrium structure as [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]]: it is a pure electrostatic field on $H$ with the point source at $p$ and the equipotential boundary condition $\varphi_I=0$ on $\Pi$; the pair $(E_I,0)$ satisfies the static electrostatic equations with source $q\delta_p$ on $H$, and the induced density is explicitly $\sigma(x_1,x_2)=-qa/[2\pi(x_1^2+x_2^2+a^2)^{3/2}]$, is absolutely integrable over the plane, and has total charge $\int_\Pi\sigma\,dS=-q$. However, the half-space conductor is not a compact conductor body: the plane is not a compact embedded hypersurface, $\Pi$ and $\{x_3<0\}$ are not among the geometric objects of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], the density $\sigma$ is not a declared stationary-sheet source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c), and the noncompact plane pairing is not an adopted compact-sheet source of that definition. As a separately specified mathematical idealization, extending $E_I$ by zero below the plane gives $\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=(q\delta_p+\sigma\delta_\Pi)/\varepsilon_0$ and $\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$, where $(\sigma\delta_\Pi)(\eta)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\sigma(x')\eta(x',0)dx'$. This verified identity does not extend the framework postulate to arbitrary noncompact sheets. The clause is the explicitly declared idealization whose exact mathematical content is (a)-(d).

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

exact_citation_checks.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the surface-measure interface inherited from [[def-em-surface-distribution]]
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\mathcal D'(U)$ be the space of
distributions on $U$ ([[def-distribution]],
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]); recall that the pairing
$\langle T,\psi\rangle$ is bilinear with no conjugation and that the
distributional partial derivatives are
$\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$
([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(a) [Fields as distributions] Locally integrable fields and source densities on
$U$ are identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

(b) [Point sources] Let $I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval,
let $z:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory whose graph map
$\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ is proper into the open set $U$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$
(coulombs). By [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],

$$\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$ with
$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=0$. If instead
$I_0=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the
absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite and both endpoint
events lie in $U$, the same formulas define distributions with

$$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$$

([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); a finite-history point source
therefore contributes an endpoint term unless that term is included
explicitly, and the pairings above exclude it only by the stated properness or
endpoint hypotheses.

(c) [Stationary-sheet sources] Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded
$C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side
$\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]],
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), and let
$\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous
with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a tangential surface current
density; the sheet is stationary). Then

$$\langle\rho_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_S\sigma(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_SK(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$: for $\psi$ with compact support the inner
integrals are continuous in $t$ on a compact parameter interval and the
functionals are bounded by
$(\sup|\sigma\psi|)\,\mathrm{area}(S)\,\mathrm{length}$ of the time projection
of the support, and likewise in the vector case. A normal sheet current (one
with $K\cdot n\ne0$), a line current and a moving sheet are not source types of
this definition.

(d) [Unrestricted weak fields and optional interface branches] The general
field class for the solution predicate (e) consists of all locally integrable
pairs $(E,B)$ on $U$, also when the source has a stationary-sheet part. No
classical one-sided trace or off-sheet $C^1$ regularity is required to define
those four distributional pairings. Additional trace hypotheses are optional
hypotheses of interface and jump results, not admission requirements of the
general weak model.

For a pointwise classical jump branch, one may additionally assume that $E,B$
are $C^1$ off $S\times I$ and, around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side
is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of
the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. These
joint one-sided extensions make the field traces and first spatial and
temporal derivatives continuous up to that side, locally uniformly on compact
cylinders.

For the broader weak-trace branch, one may instead assume the original
one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time, with the explicit additional
conditions that the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the field traces are measurable and locally
integrable on $S\times I$ for $dS\,dt$. This branch supports sheet-distribution
and almost-everywhere jump identities; spatial continuity at each time gives
pointwise spatial identities for almost every time, and joint continuity of
the jump densities gives the further all-time upgrade. Separate spatial $C^1$
traces at each time alone do not imply that joint regularity or upgrade.
Whenever such traces exist, $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ denotes their jump in the chosen
normal convention.

(e) [Weak Maxwell equations with a distributional source pair] Let $E,B$ be a
field pair of class (d), let $\rho=\rho_v+\rho_s$ and $J=J_v+J_s$ be source
distributions on $U$ whose volume parts $\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable
volume densities with the charge and current quantity types of
[[def-em-sources]] (the weak predicate requires this stated
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ regularity, not the classical continuous-source
regularity) and whose singular parts $(\rho_s,J_s)$ are point sources as in (b)
or stationary-sheet sources as in (c), and let
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]. Say that $E,B$ satisfy the weak Maxwell equations
with the source pair $(\rho,J)$ when, for every
$\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, the four pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish, all derivatives being distributional derivatives of the regular
distributions of the fields and the source pairings being those of (b) and (c).
This clause defines a solution predicate. When the singular parts vanish, its
four identities are the same as the locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. That earlier postulate explicitly excludes point
and sheet distributions and does not imply their physical adoption here;
adoption for the declared singular-source models is made separately, after
this definition. No physical field equation is deduced merely from defining
this predicate.

(f) [Scope] No product of two distributions is formed anywhere: the fields
occur only through their distributional derivatives paired with a test
function, and the source densities $\sigma,K$ occur only inside the ordinary
surface and time integrals of (b) and (c); products such as $\rho_sE$ or
$J_s\times B$ are not defined by this item. The definition asserts no existence
theorem for fields with singular sources, no conservation law (continuity for
these sources is proved separately where used) and no regularisation. Sources
that are not locally integrable and are not point or stationary-sheet sources,
moving sheets, line currents, and arbitrary products of distributions are
outside the definition.

formulation_use: where $T_{\varphi_I}$ is the regular distribution of $\varphi_I$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\delta_p$ the Dirac distribution at $p$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); moreover the field satisfies $\operatorname{div}E_I=(q/\varepsilon_0)\delta_p$ and $\operatorname{curl}E_I=0$ in $\mathcal D'(H)$, where the divergence and curl of $E_I$ are the distributional derivatives of its components ([[def-distributional-derivative]]). Thus $(E_I,0)$ is a pure electrostatic model on $H$ with the fixed-time point source $q\delta_p$, the static reading of the stationary point charge of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)).

(e) [Physics reading: ideal grounded plane in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]] the ideal grounded conducting half-space $\{x_3<0\}$ with the field $E_I$ on $H$, $E\equiv0$ below $\Pi$ and the induced density $\sigma:=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+|_\Pi=-\varepsilon_0\,\partial_3\varphi_I|_\Pi$ (using the normal $n=e_3$ from the conductor into the vacuum; $\sigma\in C^\infty(\Pi)$) is a model of the same equilibrium structure as [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]]: it is a pure electrostatic field on $H$ with the point source at $p$ and the equipotential boundary condition $\varphi_I=0$ on $\Pi$; the pair $(E_I,0)$ satisfies the static electrostatic equations with source $q\delta_p$ on $H$, and the induced density is explicitly $\sigma(x_1,x_2)=-qa/[2\pi(x_1^2+x_2^2+a^2)^{3/2}]$, is absolutely integrable over the plane, and has total charge $\int_\Pi\sigma\,dS=-q$. However, the half-space conductor is not a compact conductor body: the plane is not a compact embedded hypersurface, $\Pi$ and $\{x_3<0\}$ are not among the geometric objects of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], the density $\sigma$ is not a declared stationary-sheet source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c), and the noncompact plane pairing is not an adopted compact-sheet source of that definition. As a separately specified mathematical idealization, extending $E_I$ by zero below the plane gives $\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=(q\delta_p+\sigma\delta_\Pi)/\varepsilon_0$ and $\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$, where $(\sigma\delta_\Pi)(\eta)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\sigma(x')\eta(x',0)dx'$. This verified identity does not extend the framework postulate to arbitrary noncompact sheets. The clause is the explicitly declared idealization whose exact mathematical content is (a)-(d).
